Research umbrella: complete **Haas** mill support. We have `assets/posts/haas.cps`, but no Haas machine files (only the generic VMC), and the post has not been checked against a real NGC control.

## Open questions
1. **Models to cover first:** the common VF series (VF-2, VF-2SS), the Mini Mill and DT/DM drill-tap machines. Travels, spindle range, ATC, max feeds and rapids for each.
2. **NGC control specifics our post must match:** G187 smoothness, the setting-based work offsets (G54-G59, G154 P1-P99), the tool length offset and the program start and end conventions, the M-codes (through-spindle coolant, air blast, chip conveyor).
3. **What `haas.cps` writes today** compared with the NGC documentation: a gap list.
4. **4th and 5th axis options** (the HRT rotary, trunnions): what a later issue needs.

## Sub-issues to file (when done)
- Haas machine files (VF-2, VF-2SS, Mini Mill, DT-1/DM-1).
- `haas.cps` fixes from the gap list, with goldens.
- A test kit for a Haas owner (air cut first).

## Clean-room rules
- **Used:** the machine maker's public documentation (programming and operator manuals, spec sheets, published application notes), public G-code standards, general machining knowledge, and code-usage statistics from programs that ran on a real machine and were made by the control itself, by hand, or by non-Autodesk CAM. Files are never committed; only word and code usage is summarised.
- **Not used:** any Autodesk Fusion 360 or HSMWorks post or output (including the widely shared community posts for these machines, and NYC CNC's Fusion posts). Do not copy manual text: cite and summarise.

## Why now
mkinney, 2026-11-15: these machines are common in small professional shops, for example NYC CNC (Saunders Machine Works), which runs Tormach (supported), an Okuma GENOS M660-V (earlier an M560-V), Haas mills, and a Brother Speedio. Public sources: Okuma's Saunders Machine Works case study, the Saunders Machine Works careers page, Tormach's John Saunders pages.

**Research, not code.** Pick never takes this issue. It is answered in comments, then broken into sub-issues (AGENTS.md "needs-research").

Done means: each open question has an answered comment, the sub-issues are filed with "Part of #this", and this umbrella is closed.

I want to use CamCraft for simultaneous 5-axis machining on my self-built XYZAC milling machine.

The machine has an AC rotary table and is controlled by Mach4 with a PoKeys CNC controller. My intended application is finishing the internal freeform chamber of saxophone mouthpieces, including undercuts, with ball-nose and lollipop cutters.

body:
Found while the cut gate of v0.21.0 was red (run 43739171721, step `app heavy: pocket3d_hsm`).

What happens:
- A whole-model 3D Pocket with the Adaptive strategy and no area control clears the stock around the part out to the stock outline (#1774, PR #1780).
- On the 60 mm bore part in 70 x 70 stock, each level is then a wide ring with the part as its island.
- The HSM plan exceeds its budgets on that ring: about 600.4k outline vertices against the limit 600k (605.2k on Windows), and 124740 moves against the limit 120000.
- Offset rings cut four of the five levels. The notes name each level. The path verifies clean. There is no gouge.

Expected: the Adaptive strategy plans the stock ring within its budgets, or the budgets fit that region.

Workaround: set Tool containment to Inside on the operation. Then the pocket plans only the bore and Adaptive cuts each level.

Evidence: `crates/app/tests/pocket3d_hsm.rs`, test `the_users_bore_roughs_adaptive_level_by_level_and_verifies_clean`. The cut repaired the test with Tool containment Inside (commit `bf752be65` on `release/v0.21.0`), thus the default case has no test now.

Done means: the default whole-model Adaptive 3D Pocket on that fixture cuts each level with the Adaptive plan, with no budget note, and a test pins it.

title: post-merge.yml: let a running post-merge gate finish (cancel-in-progress: false), so a merge batch still gets complete results

body:
**The request (mkinney, 2026-11-15):** make sure the post-merge gate runs to completion even when more merges arrive, using the one-line change below.

## What happens

`.github/workflows/post-merge.yml`:

```yaml
concurrency:
  group: post-merge-${{ github.event_name == 'push' && 'main' || inputs.ref || 'main' }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
```

Each PR merge is its own push to main and starts its own run. With `cancel-in-progress: true`, each new merge cancels the run in progress. In a merge batch (N merges within one gate run, about 37 min), only the LAST run finishes:
- #1752: seven runs in a row were cancelled by later merges. The breaking merge had to be found by hand in a range of 6 merges, including the cut merge.
- #1909 and #1856 (2026-11-15): after the 10-PR bulk batch, the only result was for the tip. Each needed a manual search for the cause (#1839, and #1787 with #1793).

## Proposal (one line)

```yaml
  cancel-in-progress: false
```

With a concurrency group, GitHub keeps at most one run in progress and one pending:
- The run already in progress always finishes. It gives a full result for its commit.
- A newer merge waits as the single pending run. A still newer merge replaces it, so runs do not pile up.

For a batch of N merges this tests 2 points (the first merge and the last), not 1. Each run gives a result. The cost: more runner time on the self-hosted post-merge runner (no billed minutes), and the result for the batch tip arrives up to one gate-run later.

The comment at the top of the file (line 9, "tests only the newest head (cancel-in-progress)") must change with it. The cut-skip logic (`post-merge-skip.sh`) does not change.

## Later options (not part of this issue)

- A unique group per commit (no cancels at all): every merge is tested, but a 10-PR batch takes about 6 h on one runner.
- Bisect-when-red: when a run fails, test the merges between the last green run and this one, to find the breaking merge automatically.

body:
Add a built-in 3-axis router post for the **RichAuto DSP A11** controller in `assets/posts/richauto.cps`. Register it in `BUILTINS` in `crates/app/src/posting.rs` and pin it in `crates/app/tests/conformance.rs`.

## Context

Issue #1907 confirmed that mkinney's friend runs a **RichAuto DSP A11** handheld controller. Common Laguna Swift (`4x4`, `4x8`, `5x10`) and Grizzly CNC routers (`G0894`, `G0931`, `G0895`) also use this controller.

CamCraft's existing posts (`assets/posts/grblhal.cps`, `fanuc.cps`, `carvera.cps`, `tinyg.cps`) do not run safely on a RichAuto A11:
- `grblhal.cps` emits `G91.1`, `G94`, `G53 G0 Z...`, `T<n> M6`, and canned cycles. RichAuto A11 uses the pendant `AbsCntr` menu switch (`Off` = incremental) instead of `G91.1`, and basic router firmware can reject canned cycles or `G91.1`.
- `fanuc.cps` emits `%`, `O0001`, `T.. M6`, `G43 H..`, `G49`, `G91 G28 Z0`, and `G84` tapping.

## Specification (OEM manuals only)

1. **Units and file format:** default to `mm` (`G21`) to match RichAuto's internal metric math and avoid `G20` scale errors. Write `.nc` ASCII files with parentheses comments `(...)`. Omit `%`, `O` program numbers, and `;` comments.
2. **Preamble and arcs:** write `G21`, `G90`, `G17`, `G40`, and `G80`. Omit `G91.1`, `G94`, `G43`, and `G49`. Emit incremental `I`/`J`/`K` matching `AbsCntr = Off`. Handle `G54` cleanly (`G54` default or document `Read G54` vs `Ign G54` in post notes; handle or refuse multi-WCS safely).
3. **Spindle and warm-up:** write `S<rpm> M3`. Add a configurable spindle dwell property (`G04 P<ms>`, default `0`) so the post works alongside the pendant `Spindle Delay` setting. Document 8-step `S1`-`S8` VFD wiring in post comments.
4. **Drilling and tool changes:** expand all canned drill cycles (`G81`, `G82`, `G83`, `G73`, `G86`, `G89`) to plain `G0`/`G1` moves (using the pattern in `assets/posts/carvera.cps` and `tinyg.cps`). Refuse mid-program tool changes on the initial 3-axis manual slice (or lift Z cleanly and write `M0` with `(CHANGE TOOL T<n>)` rather than bare `T<n> M6`).
5. **Refusals and footer:** refuse `G84` tapping, `G41`/`G42` cutter compensation, and probing. Retract Z to clearance height in work coordinates, stop spindle (`M5`) and coolant (`M9` if active), and end with `M30` (no trailing `%`).

## Rules

- Clean room: use only RichAuto DSP A11 OEM documentation, RS-274 / ISO 6983 standards, and CamCraft repository patterns (`assets/posts/AGENTS.md`). Do not read or copy Autodesk, HSMWorks, or third-party CAM posts.

## Done means

- `assets/posts/richauto.cps` exists and registers in `BUILTINS` in `crates/app/src/posting.rs`.
- `crates/app/tests/conformance.rs` passes for `RichAuto DSP A11` across all mill goldens and refuses `G84`, `G41`/`G42`, and probing by name.
- Posted `.nc` output uses `G21`, incremental `I`/`J`, expanded drilling moves, `(...)` comments, safe Z retract, and `M30` with no `%`, `O` headers, `G91.1`, `G43`, or `G49`.

## Scope

  - Model stream lag scaling with thickness and traverse speed without copying any vendor table or third-party Fusion post.
  - Detect sharp corners (deflection angle) and tight curve segments on generated `WaterjetProfile` contours.
  - Compute a thickness-scaled deceleration and acceleration zone length (`3 mm` to `10 mm` range in published practice, clamped per segment).

- **Pierce and valve sequence parameters:**

title: 3D Pocket: the level law keeps only the flute radius off the walls, so a shank wider than the flutes or the holder touches walls taller than the flute length (op reads ok, the post is held)

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: area:3d
labels.description: 3D milling and finishing

body:
## What happens

A 3D Pocket level keeps the cutter centre one flute radius off the material above the level. The ladder does not look at the shank or the holder. Thus, beside a wall that is taller than the flute length, a shank that is wider than the flutes touches the wall. At a larger depth the holder touches the part too.

The generator reports the op as `ok`. Verify then names each such move as `shank_hit` (part) and each lift out of such a cut as `rapid_in_stock`. All of these findings have `blocks_post: true`, and `verify` holds the post by the op (`held_by`). Thus the output is not silent, but the user gets a toolpath that cannot post.

## Evidence

The PR #1772 takeover found this (review 5910347140 of PR #1772).

- The sample `testdata/models/sample_ap214.step` as imported, stock from the model, tool `EM-0600-4FL` (6 mm, 15 mm flute, 8 mm shank, 40 mm shank length, 44 mm holder). The part is 118 mm tall. 3D Pocket `R1` gives 306 `shank_hit` and 30 `rapid_in_stock`. All 30 rapids are vertical lifts up out of a cut. There is no gouge.
- The same `R1` path (byte-identical moves) with `flute_len` 125 and `shank_d` 6 gives no findings and `ok: true`.
- A closed cavity (40 mm block, 20 x 20 mm cavity, 30 mm deep, no open side) gives 121 `shank_hit` and 6 `rapid_in_stock` with the same tool. The result is the same with the footprint law of main (before #1749) and with the law of PR #1772. Thus the defect is on main.
- #1840 reports the same kind of shank and holder findings for the 3D Finish `S1` on the same sample.
- Pin: `crates/app/tests/shared_face_bodies.rs::the_sample_as_imported_roughs_the_3d_pocket_beside_its_silhouette` asserts this reading by name.

## Workaround

Use a tool whose flutes reach the full depth, with a shank that is not wider than the flutes. Or set Bottom Z to a depth that the tool reaches.

## What to decide

One of these, by design:

1. The ladder keeps the shank radius off the material above `level + flute_len`, and the holder radius off the material above `level + flute_len + shank_len`. Then the levels that the tool cannot reach are left as rest and named.
2. The generator refuses the levels that the tool cannot reach, by name, before it builds the path.

Do not change the verify laws. They are correct.

## Done means

A whole-model 3D Pocket with a tool that cannot reach the full depth beside a tall wall gives a path that verifies with no `shank_hit` and no `rapid_in_stock`, or a refusal or warning by name at generation. The pin in `shared_face_bodies.rs` changes to assert the new reading.

body:
## What is open

The Fanuc lathe post (`assets/posts/fanuc-lathe.cps`) can write the two-block G76 thread cycle (post option G76 cycle). The post models the control's pass schedule from public Fanuc-compatible references (GSK988TA manual, LinuxCNC G76 for the flank sign). No source that we read states four readings of that schedule. No run on a Fanuc control or on a Fanuc simulator confirms them. The PathPilot Hub simulation cannot check them, because its lathe uses the LinuxCNC one-block `G76 P.. J.. K..`.

Found in the full review of PR #517 (https://github.com/NeoTech/Camcraft/pull/517#pullrequestreview-5910390160). The readings are recorded in `docs/decisions/417-g76-matches-verified.md`.

In the table, k is the thread height and a is the tool angle of the first block (twice the flank angle).

| Item | Reading that the post uses | What a wrong reading can do | Threads affected |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Z-shift sign, and which pass sits at the programmed Z | Deeper passes move in the direction of travel (LinuxCNC sign). The post sets the start Z to `c_first - k*tan(a/2)`, so pass n starts at `start + depth_n*tan(a/2)`. | The whole thread moves axially by `k*tan(a/2)` to `2k*tan(a/2)`. For the golden `thread_g76_area.nc` (2 mm lead) that is 0.6 to 1.25 mm. This is a cut in the wrong place. | Flank threads only (a not 0) |
| 2. End-Z shift | Each pass ends at the programmed end Z. | If the control also shifts the end of each pass by `depth*tan(a/2)`, the root pass ends `k*tan(a/2)` past the end Z. At a shoulder, the tool can cut into the shoulder. | Flank threads only (a not 0) |
| 3. Minimum-depth clamp | Q(dmin) is a per-pass minimum against the previous clamped depth. | The pass count or the per-pass depth changes. The root does not change. The control can cut fewer, deeper passes than the verdict judged (the tool load is not judged). | Constant-area ladders. Equal-depth ladders (the default) are not affected. |
| 4. Rounding | Words are whole least increments. R comes from the rounded ladder and is refused beyond one increment. | The pass count is fixed. Single rungs of a long sqrt ladder can differ from the laid ones by a few increments. This is not a gouge. | Long sqrt ladders |

The default radial thread (a = 0) has no Z shift. Items 1 and 2 do not change it. Main already writes the flank angle and the flank start (#416). Thus this risk is on main now. PR #517 does not add it.

## Priority

`P3`. A wrong reading of item 1 or 2 is wrong posted G-code (a `P1` class). But no source shows that the reading is wrong, and the defect is not shown. A workaround exists: the default output is the G32 chain, which does not use the control's schedule, and the default infeed is radial. If a control run shows that item 1 or 2 is wrong, raise this issue to `P1`.

title: Fanuc-family posts write whole-number lengths with no decimal point (Z14); a control with parameter 3401#0 DPI=0 reads them as least increments

labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
What happens:
- `fanuc-lathe.cps` formats lengths with `fixed()`. This function removes the trailing zeros and also the decimal point. A whole-number length is written as `Z14`, `Z8` or `X30`, not `Z14.`.
- The Fanuc mill post does the same. Example: `crates/app/tests/golden/nc/fanuc/probe_bore_centre.nc` has `G00 Z50` and `G31 X30 Y30 Z25 F300`.
- The first-block G76 `R` word of PR #517 uses the same format. A finishing allowance of exactly 1 mm posts `R1`.

Why this is a defect:
- The published Fanuc Series 0i parameter manuals define parameter 3401 bit 0 (DPI). With DPI=0, a value with no decimal point is in the least input increment. With DPI=1 ("pocket calculator type"), it is in mm or inch.
- With DPI=0 and IS-B, `Z14` is 0.014 mm, not 14 mm. A rapid to `Z14` then goes to almost Z0. This can cause a collision.
- Other posts of this project already keep the decimal point for this reason: see the comments in `assets/posts/sinker-iso.cps` (line 53), `assets/posts/sodick-wire.cps` (line 58) and `assets/posts/AGENTS.md` (line 257).

Found during the takeover of PR #517 (lathe G76 R word). PR #517 does not cause this. Its R word follows the format of the other length words of the post.

Questions to answer:
- Which posts read the same format: fanuc, fanuc-lathe, haas, mazak, doosan-dnm, others?
- Does the project assume DPI=1? If yes, write this in each post header and in the machine documentation. If no, write each length with a decimal point (`Z14.`).

Done means: each Fanuc-family post writes a length so that the control reads the same value with DPI=0 and DPI=1, or the post header and the user documentation state the DPI=1 requirement. The goldens are updated in one commit, with a test that pins a whole-number length.

body:
Part of #874. Found while working #874 (PR #1804). Related: #637, #589, #321.

**What happens now.** PR #1804 carries the machined stock through a side-on quarter turn with a conservative read of the column body (`Body::carry_side`, `crates/sim/src/stock_sim/carry_side.rs`). The carried stock is never smaller than the real stock. The cost is this:

- A wall that the tool flank cut, or a step, is read up to one grid cell outside the real face after the turn.
- A cavity seen from the side (a pocket of the earlier setup) is filled.
- The field engine refuses a side-on turn by name (`FIELD_SIDE_CARRY_REFUSAL`).

**What a user can see.**

- The verdict can show rest of up to one cell on a face that is finished.
- The carried-fixture law (#321, `fixture_carried.rs`) can refuse a fixture that touches a turned face that was machined. The workaround is the setup's own stock.
- Rest machining in the turned setup can cut air in a filled cavity.

**The work.** Carry the stock side-on with the wall positions the engine knows, not the column pitch. One path is the field engine: re-index its 3-D bricks through the full signed permutation (`field_turn.rs` has the lattice turns only) and give it a column read that does not assume cuts along Z (`column_span`, `cut_ups`, `cut_downs`). The decision record `docs/decisions/874-side-on-carry.md` lists what was considered.

**Rule that stays.** The carried stock is never smaller than the real stock. A turn that the engine cannot carry is refused by name.

**Done means:** a plate with a contoured wall is carried side-on and the turned wall is read within the verdict tolerance, not one cell outside; a fixture in contact with that wall is not refused; a pocket of the earlier setup is still a cavity after the turn; a pinning test checks all three, and the field engine no longer refuses the side-on turn (or the issue says why it must).

body:
**The request (the user, 2026-11-14):** "create an ai chat window in CamCraft that would interact with ai thru mcp or whatever appropriate. Make sure that we help those agents with appropriate skill stuff for various ai tools like Claude, codex, Gemini, unsloth, ollama, etc."

This is a research umbrella (`needs-research`). It answers the open questions below in comments. Then it files the concrete sub-issues and closes. No code goes on this issue.

## What exists today

- `camcraft-cli mcp` is an MCP server on stdio. An agent drives one headless document.
- The app can start with `--mcp-port`, and `camcraft-cli mcp --connect <host:port>` bridges an external agent to the open window. The agent then drives the live document.
- The skill `.claude/skills/camcraft-mcp/` documents the tools for Claude Code.
- Every MCP tool calls the same undoable commands as the GUI (AGENTS.md "Commands ship with an MCP tool").

## Goal

1. **In-app chat panel.** A dock panel in CamCraft where the user types a request, for example "add a 2D pocket on the selected face with T3". An AI model answers and acts through the same MCP tool set. The panel shows each tool call and its result.
2. **Provider choice.** The user picks the model provider and the model:
   - **Cloud:** Anthropic (Claude), OpenAI (GPT/Codex models), Google (Gemini).
   - **Local:** Ollama, Unsloth Studio, LM Studio, llama.cpp server (most local servers have an OpenAI-compatible API).
3. **External agents.** Each external agent tool gets one documented way to drive the open app (`--mcp-port` plus `mcp --connect`), and a skill or instruction file in its own format:
   - Claude Code: `.claude/skills/` (exists; keep it current);
   - Codex CLI: AGENTS.md section or `.codex/` instructions;
   - Gemini / Antigravity CLI: `GEMINI.md` and `.agents/skills/`;
   - local models through Ollama or Unsloth: a short system prompt plus the tool list.

## Open questions (answer each in a comment)

1. **Panel architecture.** In-process, where the app calls the provider API and maps the MCP tools to the provider's tool-calling format? Or a separate process that speaks MCP to the app? What keeps the UI thread free (async, cancel)?
2. **One tool schema for all providers.** Map the MCP tool schemas to the Anthropic Messages tool format, the OpenAI tools format, and Gemini function declarations. Which local models do tool calling well enough? What is the fallback for a model without tool calling?
3. **Safety.**
   - Every action goes through the undoable commands.
   - The chat never posts G-code, never writes a file, and never changes a machine without a confirmation in the panel.
   - Group one chat turn as one undo step, or one step per command?
   - How does the panel show what changed?
4. **Keys and privacy.**
   - Where do API keys live (the OS keychain)?
   - What is sent to a cloud model (the project data, the model geometry)?
   - How does an offline-only setting work (local models only)?
5. **Context size.** How does a large project (many operations, big meshes) fit a model's context window? Summaries, on-demand tool reads?
6. **Skills per tool.** One source of truth for the tool docs (generated from the MCP tool list?) with per-tool wrappers, so the docs never drift from the shipped tools.
7. **Tests.** Test the panel and the tool mapping without network access (a scripted fake provider).
8. **Clean room.** Only public API documentation of each provider and the MCP specification. No code or prompts copied from other CAM products.

## Sub-issues to file (when the research is done)

- The chat panel: UI, history, tool-call display, cancel, confirmation prompts.
- The provider adapters: Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, and OpenAI-compatible local (Ollama, Unsloth, LM Studio, llama.cpp).
- The tool-schema mapping, generated from the MCP tool list.
- Keys and privacy settings, plus the offline mode.
- Skill and instruction files for Claude Code, Codex, Gemini/Antigravity and local models, generated from one source.
- Docs (REQUIRED): "Use AI with CamCraft": setup and worked examples for every provider (Claude, OpenAI/Codex, Gemini, Ollama, Unsloth Studio, LM Studio, llama.cpp) and every external agent (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini/Antigravity CLI, headless). See the comment that adds docs to the scope.

**Done means:** every open question has an answered comment, every sub-issue is filed with "Part of #this", and this umbrella is closed.

body:
The maintainer asked for this on 2026-11-14, during the v0.20.0 cut: "we need to break up that heavy lane into multiple smaller tests so we can pinpoint an exact test instead of having to run everything everytime for every little fix."

What happens now:
- `cargo xtask gate release` runs each heavy lane as one step, for example `app heavy lane (release --ignored)`.
- One step runs every `#[ignore]`d test of the crate. The v0.20.0 gate took 86.6 minutes.
- One failed test (`shared_face_bodies`, issue 1706) made the full step red. The log does not show a result for each binary at the step level.
- To check a small fix, a session must run the full lane again or write the `cargo test` command by hand.

What we want:
- The release tier plans one step for each heavy test binary (`app heavy: shared_face_bodies`, `app heavy: pocket3d_hsm`, and so on) for the app, motion and kernel heavy lanes.
- Each step has its own log file and its own pass or fail line with its wall time.
- The gate summary names each failed binary and each failed test.
- A session can run one heavy binary, or one heavy test, by name through `cargo xtask gate`.
- The release build is made one time. The steps then run the built binaries.
- A heavy test that takes more than a stated limit is reported by name with its time.

Related work:
- Issue 1702 (PR 1704) adds `--only <step>` and `--failed <gate-logs dir>`. With one step for each binary, these options select an exact binary.
- Issue 1703 covers parallel lanes. Small steps are the units that the parallel lanes run.

Done means:
- `cargo xtask gate release --dry-run` lists one step for each heavy test binary.
- A failed heavy test makes only the step of its binary red, and the summary names the test.
- `cargo xtask gate release --only "<step of one binary>"` runs that binary only.
- The `#[test]` count of the heavy lanes is the same before and after the change.
- The xtask unit tests pin the plan.
- AGENTS.md "Three gate tiers" describes the steps. The PR body carries `Process change: yes`.

Found while working #1706.

## Problem

PR #1671 turns a closed STEP body that is wound inward outward at import, and says so. The STL and OBJ importers do not do this. An inward closed STL or OBJ body keeps a negative signed volume.

`crates/motion/src/finishing3d/pencil.rs` and `deburr.rs` use the facet winding to tell a concave edge from a convex edge. An inward body swaps the two. Pencil can then trace convex edges, and deburr can select concave corners. No gouge path is known. The heights were not examined.

## Done means

- A closed, consistently wound STL or OBJ body with a negative signed volume imports turned outward, with a note in the import result and on the status line. Or the import refuses it with a clear message.
- A pinning test for each format.
- The trace of pencil and deburr heights for an inward body is recorded on this issue.

Found in M5's review of PR #1668 (#1659). The review did not block on it.

`crosses_rim` (`crates/sim/src/verify/section.rs`) counts a pass through a loop vertex as a rim crossing when the vertex's two neighbours lie on opposite sides of the move. The test is the exact sign `su * sw < 0`, with no zero band.

- The op carries a note that names the skipped band and the cause.

A note in the generator can change the CL notes of existing pockets that leave narrow slivers. Check the goldens before a change.

Done means: a model-source adaptive with a stock margin narrower than the tool cuts the band, or carries a note that names the skipped band. A test pins it.

body:
What happens: post-merge run 43535610115 (push to main at 745edc36a) ended with job `gate` = failure and job `report` = skipped. The rolling issue `main is red (post-merge gate)` was not opened or commented on.

Expected: AGENTS.md "Fixes are tested in the background": a red post-merge gate opens or comments on the rolling issue; the next green run closes it.

Cause (read from `.github/workflows/post-merge.yml` on main): the `report` job has `needs: gate` and an `if:` with no status-check function:

```
if: ${{ (needs.gate.result == 'success' || needs.gate.result == 'failure') && needs.gate.outputs.skipped != 'true' && (...) }}
```

GitHub Actions adds an implicit `success()` to a job's `if` unless it contains `always()`, `failure()`, `cancelled()` or `!cancelled()`. With a failed `needs` job the implicit `success()` is false, so the job is skipped before the expression is read. The job therefore only ever runs on green.

Suggested fix: start the condition with `always() &&` (the rest already excludes cancelled and skipped runs). One line.

Note on this particular run: its only red test was `a_lowered_cap_refuses_the_same_face_at_once` (`crates/app/tests/import_step_guard.rs`, "not within 30s"), the wall-clock flake of issue 1605, so main was not truly red here. The reporting gap is real for any failure.

A `.github/` change: the PR is read, not built, and waits for the maintainer (`needs-maintainer`). `Process change: yes` does not apply (`.github/` is not a process file).

Found by the maintenance session while watching runs.

Done means: a post-merge run whose gate fails runs `report` and opens or comments on the rolling issue; a green run after it closes that issue; a cancelled or cut-skipped run still reports nothing.

Asked for by the maintainer (2026-11-13, in chat): "we should be able to set start points on generated path and also exit points.. So the path gets regenerated to those."

What is missing: where an operation starts cutting and where it leaves is chosen by the generator alone. The user cannot say "enter here" or "leave here", for example to keep the entry mark off a visible face, to start a contour away from a clamp, or to end next to the following feature.

body:
Found while refreshing PR #1136 (#543, sinker rough and finish with undersize) over main's #544 (sinker orbit).

What happens now: #543's size law (`motion::sinker_undersize::judge`) sizes a rough or finish burn as electrode + 2 x spark gap per axis, and places the tip one undersize above the finished floor. #544's orbit moves the electrode a further `radius` sideways at the burn floor, so an orbited pass burns electrode + 2 x (gap + radius) wide. The law does not count that, so PR #1136 refuses an orbit on a rough or finish by name (`SinkerBurnOp::pass_refusal`, at command creation and at generate) instead of judging it wrongly. A plain single burn may still orbit.

What should happen: the common practice is that the electrode undersize per side covers gap + orbit, so a finish with an orbit should be judged as `e + 2(g + r) == c` (a rough: `<= c`), with the floor stand worked out so the floor is neither left short nor over-burned by the orbit, and the stock-sim verdict pinning both.

Done means: a Sinker Burn rough or finish accepts an orbit; `judge` counts the radius in the burned width; a finish with an orbit burns the cavity to size (sim verdict clean, 0 gouge, rest within the sim's resolution); an orbit that would push the walls past the cavity is refused by name; the refusal added in PR #1136 is removed; pins in `sinker_undersize` cover both.

`site/content/guide/operations.md` covers every operation kind in about 800 words. Give each kind its own reference page (or one section per kind on a page per group), so a user can look up the operation they're about to use.

Each page or section should give:
- what the operation is for and when to choose it over a neighbour (for example, adaptive vs pocket);
- the parameters that matter most, by tab, with their units and sensible starting values;
- the geometry it takes (which picks: faces, edges, chains, holes) and what a click picks;

- the refusals a user is most likely to hit, and the fix for each (link the troubleshooting page, #1244).

- 2D: facing, contour, pocket, slot, trochoidal, chamfer, engrave, trace, deburr
- 3D: adaptive, parallel, scallop, pencil, contour, and the rest of the 3D finishing set
- Holes: drill cycles, bore, thread milling, tap
- Multi-axis: rotary, swarf, flow, multi-axis contour and roughing
- Turning: facing, profiling, grooving, threading, boring, live tooling
- Probing
- Plasma
- EDM: wire and sinker (once those ship)

body:
Found while working #984.

**What happens:** the same commit plans the same part differently on two platforms. `app pocket3d_hsm::the_users_bore_roughs_adaptive_level_by_level_and_verifies_clean` (release) on ecb54b7f:

| platform | rings levels | moves / planar / arcs |
|---|---|---|
| Windows (the #850 measure, PR #865) | Z 20.000 | 5530 / 5497 / 600 |
| macOS, Apple silicon (Homebrew rustc 1.99.1) | Z 20.000 (crossing at -2.33, -2.78) | 5786 / 5753 / 651 |

macOS is deterministic run to run, so it is not hash-map order. Rust does not contract `a*b+c` into FMA unless asked, so the most likely cause is the platform libm: `f64::sin`, `cos`, `atan2`, `hypot`, `exp`, `powf` call the system math library (MSVC CRT, glibc, Apple libm), which are not correctly rounded and differ in the last place. The STEP tessellation and the adaptive planner both use them, and the planner's crossing and acceptance tests are knife edges a 16 nm change flips (#882, #982). Not yet confirmed which call sites diverge, and not run on Linux.

**Why it matters:** a toolpath (and so the posted G-code) for the same part, tool and parameters depends on the OS the user runs. Every output is still verified and a crossing plan is refused by name, so this is not a gouge; but golden counts and exact plan pins cannot hold across platforms, and a user can see a different path from the same project file on two machines.

**Possible directions (open):** route the geometry and planner transcendental calls through a pure-Rust deterministic libm (the `libm` crate is already in Cargo.lock) so every platform rounds the same; or make the planner's decisions robust to sub-micron perturbation (#882, #982). Either changes toolpaths and needs every adaptive fixture re-measured.

Done means: the cause is confirmed on a second platform (Windows or Linux run of the bore test, plus which calls diverge), and either the output is made platform-identical with goldens re-measured, or the decision not to is recorded.

Refs #984, #882, #982.

The `Thread` operation cuts only the 60-degree ISO metric / unified form: `camcraft_tools::thread_mill::form_refusal` refuses a thread mill ground to any other angle by name, and the depth is the ISO 724 constant `0.5413 x pitch`.

**What is missing**
- 55-degree Whitworth (BSW / BSP parallel): its own depth law (0.6403 x pitch, rounded crests and roots).
- Taper pipe threads (NPT, BSPT): a ride whose radius changes with Z (a conical helix in short arcs), plus the taper mill form.
- Trapezoidal and ACME forms (30 / 29 degrees).
- Pitch entry in threads per inch for unified threads.

Each form needs its depth law from the public standard (BS 84, ASME B1.20.1, ISO 2904, ASME B1.5), the form door widened to it, and the root / crest gouge readings (`operation::thread_op`) taking that depth.

**Done means:** a thread mill of each supported form threads a modelled hole of that standard, verifies clean and posts; a form with no depth law is still refused by name; pinned by goldens.

title: Picking: only feature edges, feature points and faces are pickable, never tessellation edges or hidden geometry - one rule for the whole app

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: area:ui
labels.description: User interface and picking

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

labels.name: P3
labels.description: Wrong behaviour a user hits, with a workaround; fix now

body:
Reported by the maintainer (filed by an agent), 2026-11-10.

## What happens
1. **Tessellation edges are pickable.** The selector lets you pick edges between the mesh's own triangles (at a model's vertices, inside flat faces and along smooth curves). Those aren't real model edges, and no feature should ever be built on them.
2. **Picks go through the model.** In some cases, the "select through" behaviour picks an edge (or a vertex) on the far side of the model, hidden from the user, instead of what's under the cursor.
3. **Inconsistent everywhere.** Face, vertex and edge picking behave differently from page to page: setup alignment, operation geometry, fixture mates, the WCS/origin picks, MCP picks. Users can't build a mental model of what a click will select.

## What should happen - one picking rule, used everywhere
- **Faces:** a face is a welded face, i.e. a smooth patch of triangles merged across soft edges (the `features`/`area` patches MCP's `list_features` already reports). Clicking anywhere on it picks the whole face, never a single triangle.
- **Edges:** only **feature edges** are pickable: edges where two welded faces meet at a real crease, plus open boundary edges of a sheet. Edges between triangles of the same welded face (flat-face triangulation, facets of a smooth cylinder) are never pickable. Chains follow feature edges only.
- **Points:** only **feature points** are pickable: corners where feature edges meet, the end points of open feature-edge chains, and (where a mode asks for it) arc/circle centres derived from a round feature edge. Interior mesh vertices are never pickable.
- **Visible first, never through:** a pick resolves to the front-most visible surface under the cursor (the same depth the viewport draws, perspective and ortho). An edge or point is pickable only if it is visible there (not occluded by the model, within a small screen-space tolerance of the front surface). Nothing on the far side is picked unless the user explicitly turns on a "pick through" mode, which is off by default and shown as such.
- **Snapping order near a feature:** within the pick radius, prefer point, then edge, then face, but **only** among the kinds the current tool accepts (e.g. plane alignment is faces only after #554; axis by edge or two points takes edges/points). A tool that doesn't accept edges never snaps to one.
- **One implementation:** a single picking service in the app layer (feature graph: welded faces, feature edges, feature points; visibility test against the depth the viewport uses) that every UI picker (`plane_pick`, `edge_pick`, `vertex_pick`, `axis_pick`, fixture locate, origin/WCS picks) and the MCP pick tools call. No page carries its own picking rules.

## Done means
- A shared feature-graph and pick API in the app layer, with tests:
  - a flat face's triangulation edges are not pickable;
  - a cylinder's facet edges are not pickable but its circular rim is;
  - a box corner is a pickable point, while a vertex inside a face isn't;
  - a feature edge on the far side of the part is not picked through the near face, in both perspective and ortho;
  - "pick through", when explicitly on, does pick it.
- Every UI picker and the MCP pick tools use it (no local pick logic left); UI tests on the setup page, op geometry and fixture locate confirm the behaviour.
- A short note in the user docs (#688) on what a click picks.

Related: #554 (plane picks faces only), #557 (axis by edge/points), #555 (three points), #561/#566 (fixture locate), #180 (MCP picks), #241 (selecting on complex planar faces), #613/#609/#610 (ortho rays).

title: Process changes - fork maintainers please subscribe

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: P?
labels.description: Paused: never picked until the maintainer sets a real priority

body:
**Subscribe to this issue** (the "Subscribe" button on the right) if you work from a fork of CamCraft, especially with an AI agent.

Forks sync product code only at release tags (AGENTS.md "A fork syncs from upstream at each cut tag"). But the *process* - `AGENTS.md`, the agent definitions in `.claude/agents/`, the skills in `.claude/skills/` and `scripts/gate.*` - changes between releases, and a fork's agents should follow the current rules (review labels, priority labels, release steps, and so on).

**How it works:**
- `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` holds one number. Every PR that changes a process file bumps it.
- Every such PR also adds a comment **here**: the new version, what changed, and what to pull. Subscribers get one notification per change.
- A fork's agent compares its `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` with upstream's at the start of each session and, if upstream is newer, pulls just the process files (AGENTS.md "Process files sync on every session"). Product code still waits for the next release tag.

**To pull by hand:**
```
git fetch upstream
git checkout upstream/main -- AGENTS.md .claude/agents .claude/skills .claude/PROCESS_VERSION scripts/gate.ps1 scripts/gate.sh
git commit -m "chore(process): sync process files to upstream PROCESS_VERSION <n>"
```

This issue stays open and pinned. It's labelled `P?` so no agent ever picks it up as work.

body:
Reported by a user (relayed in chat, 2026-11-07); filed by an agent.

**Setup**: laptop with a dual-GPU setup - Intel UHD (integrated) + NVIDIA Quadro P3200 (discrete), Windows.

**What happens**
1. With both GPUs enabled, the app rejects / ends up on the Intel UHD adapter and **never renders** (no viewport).
2. With the Intel GPU turned off, the NVIDIA chip **does not pick up the work** either.
3. When the app is connected to the Quadro P3200, the UI **lags 1-2 s** just rotating the empty plane view (no model loaded).

**Expected**: the app picks a working adapter (preferring the discrete GPU on hybrid systems), renders, and orbiting an empty scene is smooth on a P3200.

**Where to look** (from a read of the code, not yet reproduced):
- `crates/ui/src/egui_app/shell.rs` ~231-252: `RequestAdapterOptions { compatible_surface, ..Default::default() }` - `power_preference` is left at the default, and there is no adapter enumeration or choice by vendor/device; the fallback chain (`gpu.rs` `attempts`, `GpuPick`) only varies the *backend* (DX12 -> PRIMARY -> all), never the adapter. On Optimus/hybrid laptops the surface is presented by the integrated GPU, so a discrete adapter may not be `compatible_surface`, and the default pick can land on the Intel adapter.
- When an adapter is found but rendering never starts, there is no named refusal visible to the user - check `self.fail(...)` paths after `request_device` and surface configure (format/present-mode on the Intel adapter).
- The 1-2 s lag on an empty scene suggests a per-frame stall: present mode / vsync with a cross-adapter copy (discrete renders, iGPU presents), a blocking readback (`pollster::block_on` or a map_async wait) in the frame loop, or redraw driven by a timeout instead of input.

**Done means**
- The app enumerates adapters and logs every one it sees (name, vendor, backend, device type) at startup; the chosen one is printed by `gpu::describe(...).log_line()` already.
- On a hybrid Intel+NVIDIA laptop it renders on either GPU: prefer `PowerPreference::HighPerformance` (or a user setting to pick the adapter by name), and fall back adapter-by-adapter, not only backend-by-backend, refusing by name only when none works.
- Orbiting an empty scene on the P3200 runs at display rate (no multi-second frames); the frame-time cause is found and pinned by a test or a logged frame-time budget.

**Needs from the reporter**: the app's startup GPU log line(s) (the `gpu:` lines on stdout/stderr), Windows "Graphics settings" per-app GPU preference, NVIDIA Control Panel preferred-GPU setting, and driver versions for both GPUs.
